abstract: Highlights • EMC2 is significantly upregulated in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), an independent prognostic factor, and high EMC2 levels correlate with poor survival of NPC patients. • EMC2 suppresses ferroptosis and contributes to the progression of NPC. • A novel EMC2-TFRC axis for regulating ferroptosis. EMC2 regulates ferroptosis by mediating the ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation of TFRC.

Materials and methods
Clinical specimens
We collected 15 NPC and 15 normal nasopharyngeal epithelial tissue samples from patients who presented to Fujian Provincial Hospital between February 2021 and December 2021. Eight NPC and eight normal tissues were used for label-free quantitative proteomics and the remaining tissues were subjected to Western blot. Additionally, 16 paraffin-embedded NPC specimens and 6 paraffin-embedded normal nasopharyngeal epithelial specimens were retrospectively obtained from the Fujian Provincial Hospital between July 2019 and July 2021. All enrolled patients provided written informed consent. The Accreditation Committee of Fujian Provincial Hospital approved the collection of human samples.
NPC tissue microarrays
NPC tissue microarrays (#NPC1401) were procured from Zhuohao Medical Science and Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). After excluding the samples with missing tissue sites, tissue microarrays contain comprehensive clinicopathological and follow-up data from 121 paraffin-embedded NPC specimens.
Label‑free quantitative proteomics
Label-free quantitative proteomics was conducted in Genechem Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Briefly, the samples were lysed by SDT buffer, then subjected to sonication and boiling. The supernatant was obtained after centrifugation, followed by protein quantification using BCA assay. Protein samples were reduced, ultrafiltered, and trypsinized. The peptides were desalted using C18 cartridges and the samples were concentrated and redissolved in formic acid. An Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) combined with Easy nLC was used for liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis. SpectroMine 2.6 software was used to analyze MS data. The MS data were searched against the UniProt database. The peptide and protein identification involved setting the false discovery rate (FDR) to 0.01. Protein abundance was computed according to normalized spectral protein intensity. Finally, the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified using a
P
-value (Student's
t
-test) <0.05 and fold change >2 or <0.5.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Paraffin-embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated. Antigen retrieval was performed using citric sodium buffer (pH 6.0) via pressure cooking. Nonspecific binding and endogenous peroxidase activity were blocked using an UltraSensitive™ SP IHC Kit (MXB biotechnologies). Sections were incubated with primary antibodies (Table S1) overnight at 4.0 °C. Sections were counterstained with diaminobenzidine and hematoxylin, dehydrated, cleared, and imaged. Two pathologists blindly evaluated each section semi-quantitatively and assigned a score. The staining intensity was negative, weak, medium, or strong, and the percentage of tumor cells at each staining intensity was determined (1–100 %). The IHC scores were calculated using the following formula: [(%weak cells) × 1+(%medium cells) × 2+(%strong cells) × 3]. The median score for EMC2 staining in NPC tissues microarrays was determined to be 1.2. Samples were divided into Low (score ≤1.2) and High (score >1.2) groups.
Public datasets
EMC2 expression in pan-cancer was obtained from Sangerbox database, an online platform for TCGA data analysis (
http://vip.sangerbox.com/
). The survival analysis of pan-cancer was assessed using GEPIA2 (
http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/
) and Kaplan-Meier plotter (
http://kmplot.com/analysis/
).
Cell culture and treatment
The normal human nasopharyngeal cell line (NP69) and human nasopharyngeal carcinoma cell lines (CNE1, CNE2, and 5–8F) were sourced from Cell Biology Laboratory, Central South University, while c666–1 was purchased from Meisen-CTCC (Hangzhou, China). These cell lines were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium with 10 % fetal bovine serum, maintained in an incubator with an atmosphere of 5 % CO
2
at 37 °C. For drug treatment, the indicated cells were treated with reagents (Table S2) as need.
Lentiviral vectors, small interfering RNA and cell transduction
To knock down and overexpress EMC2, EMC2 RNAi lentiviral vectors, CMV-MCS-3flag-EF1a-hScarlet-T2A-puromycin lentiviral vector of EMC2 cDNA, and corresponding control lentiviral vectors were purchased from Genechem Co., Ltd. Briefly, cells were maintained in 6-well plates at 20–30 % confluence. Lentivirus was transduced into 5–8F or c666–1 cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 20 or 50 for 24 h The stably transfected cell lines were screened with 3 or 5 µg/mL puromycin for two weeks.
To overexpress the transferrin receptor (TFRC) in 5–8F cells of overexpressing EMC2, the pHBLV-CMV-TFRC—HIS-EF1-NEO lentiviral vector was manufactured by Hanbio Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China), HBLV-NEO lentiviral vector as control. The stable cells demonstrating TFRC overexpression were screened using 600 µg/mL G418 for two weeks. TFRC expression was inhibited in 5–8F cells with EMC2 knockdown by siRNA against TFRC (siTFRC), which was synthesized by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China), Scrambled siRNA as control. When cell confluence reached approximately 50–60 %, the cells were transfected with 50 nM siTFRC mixed with Lipofectamine 3000 following the manufacturer's guides. Target and control sequences are listed in Table S3.
Cell viability assays
Cell viability was detected by the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8). Cells (5000 cells/well) were incubated for 24 h in 96-well plates. After the indicated treatment and duration, 100 µl of medium with 10 % CCK-8 solutions was added, then cells were incubated for 1.5 h at 37 °C. Cell viability (%) was calculated from the absorbance of samples at 450 nm using a microplate reader.
Quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR)
The total RNA of the indicated cells was isolated using the NucleoZOL reagent (Macherey-Nagel). Next, total RNA was reverse-transcribed to synthesize cDNA using the PrimeScript™ RT reagent Kit (Takara). RT-qPCR was carried out using TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ (Tli RNaseH Plus) (Takara) on a LightCycler® 480 Fluorescence Quantitative System (Roche). The gene expression was normalized using GAPDH, and the 2
−ΔΔCt
method was performed for quantitative analysis. The primer sequences are shown in Table S4.
Transwell assays
Cell migration and invasion capacity were evaluated using Transwell inserts (Corning) coated or uncoated with 20 µg Matrigel (ABW) in 24-well plates. Briefly, 1 × 10
4
cells were grown in the upper chamber with 200 µl PBS-free medium, while 500 µl of complete medium was supplemented in the lower chamber for 24 h Cells crossing the membrane were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde, and the cells with crystal violet staining were counted using a microscope.
Transmission electron microscopy
The cells were harvested and fixed with 4 % glutaraldehyde and 2.5 % paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). Standard subsequent procedures, including post-fixation, dehydration, resin embedding, and sectioning, were performed. Next, sections were stained with uranium acetate and lead citrate, and images of cellular mitochondrial morphology were obtained by a Hitachi HT7800 transmission electron microscopy (Tokyo, Japan).
Tandem mass tag (TMT) quantitative proteomics
TMT quantitative proteomics was performed by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Briefly, control and EMC2 knockdown 5–8F cell samples (three samples/group) were lysed and centrifuged. The supernatant of proteins was extracted and reduced, followed by alkylated with sufficient iodoacetamide. After the extracted proteins were trypsinized, peptides were desalted and collected using a C18 cartridge. Desalted peptides were labeled using the TMTpro™ 18-plex Label Reagent Set (Thermo Fisher). The TMT-labeled peptide mix was fractionated by a C18 column. Proteomic analyses were performed using an EASY-nLCTM 1200 UHPLC system coupled with a Q Exactive™ HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher). Samples of each fraction were injected into pre-column and separated on an analytical column, and a mass spectrometer analyzed the isolated peptides. Proteins were identified and quantified based on the UniProt database by a Proteome Discoverer (HFX and 480, Thermo Fisher). The identified proteins were retained with FDR <1.0 %. The results of protein quantitation were tested by
t
-tests. DEPs were defined as fold-change >1.2 or <0.83 and
P
-value <0.05. Based on the DEPs, the Volcano plot, heatmap, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) were analyzed.
Additionally, possible target proteins for EMC2 were analyzed based on the overlaps between DEPs and a previous dataset of EMC2-immunoprecipitation (IP) proteins [
21
].
Western blot and co-IP
Total protein from tissues or cells was isolated by RIPA buffer (Solarbio) with protease inhibitors. The protein concentration was measured by BCA assay. After boiling in loading buffer, proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore). After blocking, the electroblotted samples were incubated with indicated primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The samples were hybridized with secondary antibodies (1:5000, Bioworld). Protein levels were determined and visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence kit (Smart-Lifesciences) on a ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad).
Co-IP assay was conducted by the Pierce™ Classic Magnetic IP/Co-IP Kit (Thermo Fisher). Cells were lysed and centrifuged to collect soluble fractions. Indicated samples were incubated with antibodies for IP overnight at 4 °C. Immunoprecipitated proteins were washed and eluted after capture with protein A/G-magnetic beads, followed by Western blot. The primary antibodies were listed in Table S1.
Immunofluorescence analysis
Cells were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde and permeabilized with 0.2 % Triton X-100 on culture slides. Cells were blocked with goat serum for 1 h and then incubated with primary antibodies (Table S1) overnight at 4 °C, followed by incubation with fluorescent secondary antibodies (1:500, Abcam) at dark for 1 h Nuclei were labeled with DAPI. The fluorescence distribution of target proteins was monitored by a confocal laser-scanning microscope (Leica TC SP8).
Measurement of cell death
Cell death was detected using the Pharmingen™ FITC Annexin V Apoptosis Detection Kit I (BD). Briefly, the indicated cells were trypsinized, collected, and resuspended with Binding Buffer. Approximately 1 × 10
5
cells in Binding Buffer were incubated with 5 µl of FITC Annexin V in the dark for 15 min. Annexin
V
+ cells (dead cells) were quantified using a BD Accuri C6 Plus flow cytometer and FlowJo™ 10 software.
Lipid peroxidation measurement
Cellular lipid peroxidation was measured using C11-BODIPY 581/591 (GlpBio). Cells were grown in 6-well plates and incubated by 2 ml medium containing 5 μM C11-BODIPY 581/591 for 30 min at 37 °C. Cells were trypsinized, washed, and resuspended in PBS. The cell samples were analyzed using a flow cytometer.
Malondialdehyde (MDA) and GSH/GSSG measurement
MDA and GSH/GSSG in cells or tissues were assessed using an MDA assay kit (Beyotime) and a GSH and GSSG assay kit (Beyotime), respectively, following the manufacturer's guidelines.
Animal experiments
Five-week-old male BALB/c nude mice were sourced from SLAC Laboratory Animal Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) and housed in a specific pathogen-free facility. All animal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of Hainan Medical University and conducted following the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Xenograft mouse models of two groups (
n
= 6 mice/group) were generated by injecting 1 × 10
6
stably knocked-down EMC2 5–8F cells or control-transfected 5–8F cells subcutaneously into the right flank. Tumor volume was measured as length (L) × width (W)
2
× 1/2 every 3 days. After tumor implantation for 27 days, mice were euthanized, and the tumors were collected, weighed, and imaged, followed by MDA assays, GSH/GSSG detection, and IHC analysis.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software) and SPSS 22.0 (IBM). Differences between the two groups were compared using a two-tailed unpaired Student's
t
-test. One-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare multiple groups. The association between EMC2 levels and clinicopathological features was analyzed by χ
2
-test. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models identified prognostic factors. Overall survival (OS), relapse-free survival (RFS), and disease-free survival (DFS) curves were constructed using the Kaplan-Meier (K-M) method. Statistical significance was
P
-value <0.05.

Introduction
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is an epithelial malignancy that originates in the nasopharynx and commonly affects the head and neck [
1
]. Approximately 10–20 % of NPC patients experience local recurrence or distant metastasis, often attributed to resistance developed during chemoradiotherapy [
2
]. Patients with locally advanced NPC have a poor prognosis because of increased tumor invasion and metastasis. Numerous genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic changes occur during the development of NPC [
3
]. The molecular mechanisms underlying NPC tumorigenesis and progression are not well elucidated.
Ferroptosis is programmed cell death featuring iron-dependent accumulation of lipid peroxidation [
4
]. It differs from other forms of cell death, such as necroptosis and apoptosis, at biochemical, morphological, and genetic levels. The distinctive characteristics of cellular ferroptosis include organelle shrinkage, condensed mitochondrial membranes, and absent mitochondrial crest [
4
]. Ferroptosis is associated with various pathological and physiological processes and its inactivation drives tumorigenesis and progression [
5
,
6
]. The regulation of ferroptosis is aberrant in tumors, with dysregulated molecules like p53, lysine methyltransferase 2B, and cysteine desulfurase inhibiting ferroptosis in tumors [
[7]
,
[8]
,
[9]
]. Increasing evidence suggests that ferroptosis significantly influences NPC. For example, Epstein-Barr virus infection induces ferroptosis insensitive and chemoresistance in NPC [
10
].
Endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein complex 2 (EMC2) is a significant core subunit of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein complex located on the cytoplasmic side, which inserts newly synthesized membrane proteins into the ER membrane [
[11]
,
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
]. EMC2 contains a tetratricopeptide repeat domain mediating protein-protein interactions in various pathways [
[15]
,
[16]
,
[17]
]. EMC2 has been implicated in erastin-induced ferroptosis [
4
,
6
]. EMC2 is highly expressed in breast cancer and esophageal adenocarcinoma and is associated with the prognosis of patients [
[18]
,
[19]
,
[20]
]. However, functional and mechanistic studies of EMC2 in ferroptosis, especially in NPC, remain to be conducted.
In this study, we observed EMC2 levels and assessed its clinical significance in NPC. Moreover, in vitro and in vivo experiments were performed to evaluate the key role of EMC2 in ferroptosis and NPC progression. We explored the potential mechanisms and pathways of EMC2 regulating ferroptosis. These results provide further insight into EMC2 as a promising biomarker and therapeutic target for NPC.

Result
EMC2 is upregulated in NPC and negatively related to prognosis
To identify essential proteins in NPC, quantitative proteomic analysis was conducted in NPC and normal nasopharyngeal epithelial tissues. We identified 283 dysregulated proteins in NPC, and EMC2 expression was markedly higher in NPC tissues than in normal nasopharyngeal epithelial tissues (
Fig. 1
A and B). We also observed significant upregulation of EMC2 in 17 out of 34 tumor datasets from TCGA and GTEx (Figure S1A). Analyses using Kaplan-Meier Plotter revealed that high EMC2 expression was associated with poor OS or RSF in 8 tumors (Figure S1B-I). These analytic results suggest that dysregulated EMC2 is prevalent and potentially oncogenic in tumors. We further verified the highly expressed EMC2 in NPC using Western blot and IHC (
Fig. 1
C, S1 J). We performed IHC staining of EMC2 in the NPC tissues microarray of 121 patients to analyze the correlation between EMC2 levels and the clinicopathological features (
Fig. 1
D). We confirmed that high EMC2 levels were markedly related to tumor invasion, lymphatic metastasis, distant metastasis, and locally advanced and advanced stages (stages II-IV) (
Table 1
). Furthermore, stage II-IV and high EMC2 expression were confirmed as independent risk factors for OS in NPC by univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses (
Table 2
). Cox regression analysis also identified that age, stage II-IV disease and high EMC2 expression were independent risk factors for RFS in NPC (
Table 3
). High EMC2 levels had dramatically shorter OS and RFS in NPC patients (
Fig. 1
E and F). In addition, EMC2 was increased in HNSC from TCGA HNSC datasets (
Fig. 1
G). Analysis of the GEPIA2 database showed that high EMC2 expression was correlated with poor DFS in HNSC (
Fig. 1
H). Based on these results, we speculated that EMC2 is a key protein in NPC.

Ferroptosis is inhibited in NPC
As is well-known, the suppression of ferroptosis largely contributes to the development of tumors. IHC staining for 4-Hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) was conducted to assess lipid peroxidation levels in NPC and normal nasopharyngeal epithelial tissues. The intensity of 4-HNE staining was lower in NPC tissues (
Fig. 2
A). NP69 and NPC cells (CNE1, CNE2, c666–1, and 5–8F cells) were treated with various concentrations of erastin (a ferroptosis inducer) for 24 h CCK-8 assays indicated that the IC50 of NPC cells for erastin was higher than that of NP69, and erastin-induced cell death was remarkably lower in NPC cells (
Fig. 2
B). Moreover, Western blot analysis suggested that glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and cystine/glutamate transporter (SLC7A11) levels were upregulated, while TFRC levels were downregulated in NPC cells (
Fig. 2
C). These findings underscore the inhibition of ferroptosis in NPC. We hypothesized that EMC2, a ferroptosis-related molecule [
4
], inhibits ferroptosis and promotes NPC progression.

Fig. 3

Fig. 3
H and I). These results suggest that EMC2 exerts a vital influence on ferroptosis suppression and tumor progression in NPC.

EMC2 interferes with the sensitivity of NPC cells to cisplatin
In addition, NPC cells were treated with cisplatin after knocking down or overexpressing EMC2. CCK-8 and colony formation assays showed that the viability and proliferation of NPC cells treated with cisplatin were significantly decreased after EMC2 knockdown (Figure S4A-C). Conversely, EMC2 overexpression notably increased the viability and proliferation of 5–8F cells treated with cisplatin (Figure S4D, E). Above results suggest that targeting the EMC2-regulated ferroptosis renders NPC more sensitive to cisplatin.
EMC2 knockdown enhances ferroptosis and suppresses tumor growth in vivo
Xenograft tumor models were constructed to further assess the function of EMC2 in NPC. Control or EMC2 knockdown 5–8F cells were subcutaneously transplanted into nude mice. Detection of tumor volume confirmed that EMC2 knockdown substantially reduced the size of tumors (
Fig. 4
I). EMC2 knockdown remarkably reduced tumor weight (
Fig. 4
J). A lower GSH/GSSG ratio and elevated MDA concentration were checked in tumors with EMC2 knockdown (
Fig. 4
K and L). Consistently, EMC2 knockdown observably enhanced 4-HNE staining and decreased Ki67 staining in tumor xenograft samples (
Fig. 4
M). The results suggest that EMC2 inhibits ferroptosis and promotes NPC progression in vivo.
EMC2 interacts with TFRC and promotes the degradation of TFRC in NPC cells
To elucidate the mechanism of EMC2-regulated ferroptosis in NPC, we performed TMT quantitative proteomics in EMC2 knockdown and control 5–8F cells. Analysis of the DEPs revealed 350 upregulated and 156 downregulated proteins in 5–8F cells following EMC2 knockdown (
Fig. 5
A and B). Moreover, KEGG and GSEA enrichment analyses substantiated that the ferroptosis pathway was activated after EMC2 knockdown, indicating that EMC2 regulates ferroptosis in NPC cells (
Fig. 5
C and D). To further explore the potential direct interactors regulated by EMC2 among the DEPs, we searched and downloaded a dataset of EMC2-IP proteins obtained using affinity purification coupled with mass spectrometry (AP-MS) in a previous study [
21
]. We observed an overlap between the EMC2-IP dataset and the DEPs, revealing 13 proteins were directly interacted with EMC2 (
Fig. 5
E). Among them, TFRC, a core ferroptosis regulator, attracted our attention. We performed IHC staining of EMC2 and TFRC in NPC tissues and bioinformatics analysis of our proteomics data and
GSE102394
dataset to explore the correlation between EMC2 and TFRC in clinical specimens. These results indicated that TFRC was negatively correlated with EMC2 (Figure S5A-C), which was consistent with Western blot results that EMC2 downregulated TFRC expression. Surprisingly, the interaction between EMC2 and TFRC was identified in control and EMC2-overexpressing 5–8F cells by co-IP assays (
Fig. 5
F). We also observed co-location of EMC2 and TFRC in 5–8F and c666–1 cells (
Fig. 5
G).

EMC2 regulates ferroptosis through TFRC in NPC cells
Next, we determined whether EMC2 inhibits ferroptosis by mediating TFRC downregulation. We transfected siTFRC into 5–8F cells of EMC2 knockdown to interfere with TFRC upregulation (
Fig. 6
A). Decreased cell viability and increased cell death were largely rescued after interfering with TFRC in EMC2 knockdown 5–8F cells (
Fig. 6
B and C). Moreover, after interfering with TFRC, EMC2 knockdown in 5–8F cells reduced lipid peroxidation to levels similar to those detected in control 5–8F cells (
Fig. 6
D). The increased ACSL4 and decreased GPX4 and Ferritin levels were significantly reversed in EMC2 knockdown 5–8F cells after transfection with siTFRC (
Fig. 6
E). The reduced GSH/GSSG ratio and accumulation of MDA induced by EMC2 knockdown were mainly reversed by interference with TFRC (
Fig. 6
F and G). In addition, TFRC expression was restored in EMC2-overexpressing 5–8F cells following lentivirus infection (
Fig. 6
H). TFRC restoration mostly abolished the inhibition of ferroptosis in EMC2-overexpressing cells, as manifested by decreased cell viability, increased cell death, and lipid peroxidation accumulation (
Fig. 6
I–K). TFRC restoration reversed the downregulation of ACSL4 and the upregulation of GPX4 and Ferritin in EMC2-overexpressing 5–8F cells (
Fig. 6
L). The elevated GSH/GSSG and lowered MDA concentration were consistently recused by upregulating TFRC in EMC2-overexpressing 5–8F cells (
Fig. 6
M and N). Overall, these results suggest that the EMC2-TFRC axis regulates ferroptosis in NPC.

Discussion
The 5-year survival rate for NPC worldwide is approximately 50–72 % over the past 20 years [
22
]. Most patients with NPC remain asymptomatic until the cancer reaches a locally advanced stage. Although multiple treatment strategies can improve the therapeutic outcomes, some patients with locally advanced NPC often sustain tumor and recurrence, resulting in a poor prognosis. The pathophysiology of NPC needs to be fully elucidated. Understanding the mechanism of cell death inhibition is significant for designing treatment strategies for NPC. In the study, dysregulated proteins were detected in NPC by proteomic analysis, and EMC2 was highly expressed in NPC. EMC2 is a core subunit of the conserved ER-resident complex that plays a significant character in the biological processes of various membrane proteins [
23
,
24
]. Our study demonstrated that EMC2 levels are related to tumor invasion, lymphatic metastasis, distant metastasis, and clinical stage of NPC. EMC2 is an independent risk factor for NPC prognosis and high EMC2 expression indicates poor OS and RFS in NPC patients. Moreover, EMC2 expression is increased in HNSC and is related to patient survival. Previous studies have also noted that high EMC2 levels correlate with shorter survival in breast cancer and esophageal adenocarcinoma [
[18]
,
[19]
,
[20]
]. This conclusive evidence demonstrates the significant role of EMC2 in NPC.
Although distinct from apoptosis, necroptosis, and autophagy, ferroptosis is considered crucial for the tumorigenesis, progression and treatment of tumors [
25
,
26
]. Mounting studies have shown that ferroptosis is a tumor-suppressive mechanism that mediates cell death [
[27]
,
[28]
,
[29]
]. Cancer can sustain survival and promote progression by inactivating cell death pathways [
30
]. In our study, we observed the inhibition of ferroptosis in NPC, including lower levels of 4-HNE staining, insensitivity of erastin, and dysregulation of ferroptosis-related proteins. Recent studies have pinpointed that ferroptosis inhibition promotes NPC development and treatment resistance [
31
,
32
]. Thus, inactive ferroptosis plays a pivotal part in NPC progression. We confirmed that EMC2 was remarkably upregulated in NPC cells at both the mRNA and protein levels. Moreover, EMC2 knockdown drove ferroptosis-related events and repressed NPC cells migration and invasion. Overexpressing EMC2 dramatically suppressed ferroptosis in NPC cells and enforced tumor progression. EMC2 knockdown inhibited NPC growth and improved ferroptosis in vivo. Previous studies indicated that EMC2 is related to ferroptosis in tumors [
4
]. EMC2 is a core subunit of ER membrane proteins. ER has been reported to be a crucial subcellular organelle for lipid peroxidation in ferroptosis and may be a key determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity [
33
,
34
]. Another study demonstrated the involvement of ER stress-mediated autophagy activation in ferroptosis [
35
]. Based on these evidences, we believe that EMC2 plays a role in cellular ferroptosis. Our findings are the first to demonstrate that EMC2 negatively regulates ferroptosis and promotes NPC progression.
ROS play a crucial role in ferroptosis. Chemotherapeutics can increase ROS, contributing to cancer cells and treatment resistance. Chemotherapeutic drugs disrupt the redox balance, making tumor cells more susceptible to ferroptosis [
10
,
36
]. Cisplatin initiates ferroptosis primarily by depleting intracellular GSH [
37
]. Conversely, gemcitabine-induced ferroptosis resistance, through upregulation of GPX4, can inhibit tumor cell death [
38
]. Additionally, activating ferroptosis with inducers or genetic manipulation enhances the efficacy of these chemotherapeutic drugs [
10
,
[36]
,
[37]
,
[38]
], potentially offering new insights for de-escalation strategies in NPC treatment. In our study, EMC2 knockdown enhanced ferroptosis in NPC cells and enhanced the anti-cancer effect of cisplatin, suggesting that EMC2 is a promising therapeutic target for combination with traditional chemotherapeutic drugs in NPC treatment.
Emerging molecular regulatory pathways of ferroptosis including the BAP1-SLC7A11 pathway, GPX4 pathway, NRF2-ferritin pathway, and p53-TFRC pathway, have been revealed [
28
,
[39]
,
[40]
,
[41]
]. However, the major ferroptosis regulatory pathways of EMC2 have not yet been elucidated. We conducted TMT quantitative proteomics to detect the DEPs in NPC cells following EMC2 knockdown. Notably, the identified DEPs were enriched in ferroptosis pathways, underscoring the significant role of EMC2 in ferroptosis. Previous studies informed that EMC2 is necessary to stabilize many multi-pass membrane proteins [
11
], and the tetratricopeptide repeat domain is involved in protein interactions [
17
]. Thus, EMC2 likely regulates ferroptosis by interacting with the downstream proteins. Based on the overlap between DEPs caused by EMC2 knockdown and the EMC2-IP proteins obtained from another study, TFRC attracted our attention and interest. A previous study confirmed that the upregulated expression of TFRC can serve as a marker of ferroptosis and enhance cellular ferroptosis [
42
]. Increasing studies have shown that transferrin-associated receptors significantly regulate ferroptosis [
43
,
44
]. Our experiments identified the interaction and co-location of EMC2 and TFRC in NPC cells. Furthermore, this study verified that EMC2 knockdown upregulated TFRC, whereas EMC2 overexpression decreased TFRC levels. These results provide reliable evidence that EMC2 interplays with TFRC and negatively regulates TFRC levels in NPC cells.
In addition, we found that EMC2 did not apparently affect the mRNA level of TFRC but regulated its protein levels. The evidence supports that EMC2 regulates TFRC levels by post-translational modifications. Almost all proteins in eukaryotic cells are post-translationally modified by ubiquitination, phosphorylation, acetylation, and methylation. The ubiquitin-proteasome pathway is critical for protein degradation and is mainly mediated by ubiquitin in cancer [
45
]. Previous research has summarized that there is a ubiquitin system in ER that degrades unwanted proteins to maintain protein homeostasis [
46
]. EMC2 has been found to interact with E3 ligases [
47
]. In this study, we validated that the proteasome inhibitor MG132 could reverse the downregulation of TFRC levels caused by EMC2 overexpression in NPC cells. Moreover, the ubiquitination of TFRC was increased in EMC2-overexpressing NPC cells. These studies further indicate that EMC2 downregulates TFRC via the ubiquitin-proteasomal pathway. A previous study also corroborated that ubiquitin ligase E3 attaches to TFRC, resulting in its proteasomal degradation, thereby repressing ferroptosis [
48
], which supports our findings. Collectively, EMC2 targets TFRC, resulting in the ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation of TFRC.
Furthermore, we investigated the vital regulatory of the EMC2-TFRC axis in ferroptosis. Reducing the increased TFRC levels could effectively reverse the enforced ferroptosis events in NPC cells following EMC2 knockdown. Conversely, augmenting the decreased TFRC induced by EMC2 overexpression could rescue the suppressed ferroptosis. Altogether, our data indicate that EMC2 regulates ferroptosis through TFRC in NPC. We have uncovered a novel regulatory axis involving EMC2-TFRC that mediates ferroptosis in NPC.
In summary, our findings are the first to highlight the carcinogenic role of EMC2 in NPC progression via ferroptosis suppression. This study suggests that increased EMC2 levels are associated with malignant manifestations of NPC, and EMC2 is an independent risk factor for prognosis. Moreover, our study unveils the mechanism by which EMC2 regulates ferroptosis via TFRC and sheds new light on promising biomarkers and therapeutic targets for NPC.
